analysis.one_liner: Bans evictions and foreclosures in federally declared disaster areas until unemployment falls below 8.5%.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2020 and referred to two House committees, where it received no hearing, vote, or floor action before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar landlords from evicting tenants for nonpayment of rent, charging late fees, or forcing them out in any federally declared disaster area, and would bar mortgage servicers from starting foreclosures on federally backed home loans unless the property is vacant or abandoned. The protections would stay in place until the disaster declaration ends or the state's unemployment rate has been under 8.5% for two straight months — whichever comes later. Because it applied to disasters already declared, it would have covered the COVID-19 emergency immediately.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and homeowners in declared disaster areas, particularly during periods of high unemployment. A tenant could not be taken to eviction court for unpaid rent, hit with late fees, or pressured to leave, and a homeowner with a federally backed mortgage could not have foreclosure proceedings started against an occupied home. Because the bill applied to disasters in effect at enactment, people behind on rent or mortgage payments during the COVID-19 emergency would have been covered right away.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters and homeowners in disaster areas

how_it_helps.text: Bars mortgage servicers from starting any foreclosure process, judgment, or foreclosure sale on a federally backed mortgage in a disaster area, unless the property is vacant or abandoned.

Bars landlords in a disaster area from filing eviction actions for nonpayment of rent or fees, charging late fees or penalties for nonpayment, or requiring a tenant to vacate, and requires a 30-day notice to vacate after the moratorium ends.

Keeps the protections in place until the later of the end of the disaster declaration or a certification that the state's unemployment rate has been below 8.5% for two consecutive months, so protections last as long as joblessness remains high.
Applies to any disaster declaration in effect on the date of enactment, which included the COVID-19 national emergency then underway.

analysis.who_pays: Landlords would lose the ability to evict nonpaying tenants or collect late fees during the moratorium, while rent obligations kept accruing; mortgage servicers and lenders would be unable to begin foreclosure on occupied federally backed homes. Neither receives compensation under the bill.

drawbacks.text: The moratorium defers but does not cancel what is owed: rent and mortgage payments continue to accrue during the disaster, so households can emerge with a large debt load the moment the moratorium lifts.

The bill contains no relief fund or compensation for landlords, whose rental income is blocked during the moratorium — a strain that falls hardest on small landlords relying on a few units for income.
The foreclosure ban covers only federally backed mortgage loans, leaving foreclosures on other loans unrestricted in disaster areas.

The unemployment-based termination means the moratorium can run long after the disaster itself has passed — which supporters intended as a safeguard, but opponents would call an open-ended freeze on landlords and lenders tied to a statewide, not local, jobless rate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households at risk of losing their homes during a disaster with high unemployment, the protections are strong and direct. The main costs fall on landlords and servicers as deferred collections, and the bill's real weakness is that it postpones the debt rather than relieving it, setting up a wave of evictions and foreclosures the moment the moratorium ends unless separate aid follows. It is a targeted stopgap, not a permanent solution.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2020 and sent to the Financial Services and Education and Labor Committees, which took no further action on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Val Demings of Florida introduced the Federal Disaster Housing Stability Act of 2020 on September 1, 2020, joined by seven original cosponsors.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Financial Services and, in addition, to the Committee on Education and Labor; no further action appears in its history.
The bill never received a committee hearing or vote, a floor vote, or Senate action, and expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
At the time of introduction, the COVID-19 national emergency was in effect, so the bill's moratorium would have applied nationwide immediately upon enactment.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and mortgage servicers were spared the temporary eviction and foreclosure limits, while renters and homeowners in disaster areas received no federal protection from the bill — leaving them to rely on whatever separate, temporary measures existed at the time.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew only Democratic support (a sponsor plus 8 of 231 House Democrats, no Republican cosponsors) and never reached a vote, so no roll call shows how the chamber would have split.

industries.note: In a declared disaster area, landlords could not file evictions for unpaid rent, charge late fees, or demand that tenants leave, and could not even issue a notice to vacate until the moratorium ended. Rent owed continued accruing, so the cost to landlords was deferred income rather than forgiven debt, with no compensation in the bill.

Servicers of federally backed mortgages in disaster areas would have been barred from initiating foreclosure or executing foreclosure sales on occupied properties. This delayed collections and foreclosure activity during the moratorium period.
